I'll start this off with saying the game is fully playable on Deck without a single crash. Type in "MESA_LOADER_DRIVER_OVERRIDE=zink %command%" without the quotation marks in your launch settings, and just make sure MSAA is Off and you don't set your Draw Distance any higher than mid, and you can max out everything else. No need for a specific version of Proton. Runs like a beauty. Anyway, onto the actual review:

TY 3 is a weird game for me. I know full well it's the least liked of the original trilogy, and I can understand why people might feel that way. Keeping circumstances in mind, the biggest criticism and simultaneously the best praise I can give TY 3 is that it left me wanting more. This is easily my favourite game in the series, rushed development and all. The music is fantastic (as usual), the touchups to the combat are enough to make it fun, and being able to put together your own broken 'rangs with the stone system is just fun. It isn't long before you go from having to be conservative with your loadouts to decimating everything with 'rangs you can throw rapidfire that autotarget enemies and explode, and it feels good. The story's charming enough, though the characters are what really shines. It's clear that the game had to be rushed out the door, and it's one of the most unfortunate things in gaming to me. If it had been allowed a little more time in the oven, it would have been close to perfect for me. Still, it clicked, and it clicked hard. 

If you want more of a traditional collectahon, you're not going to get it here. The platforming isn't anything crazy, especially compared to the previous games, but it doesn't need to be. The only parts I found frustrating were some of the flying missions, but never enough to make me put the game down, and I came to appreciate them when they popped up. I honestly feel like they're a step up from TY 2's copter segments once you get the hang of the controls, but I digress. I don't have anything to really complain that couldn't just be summed up as wanting more. 

I love running around the two overworld maps in the dumb crab blowing everything up; I wish there were more overworld maps to explore. I love putting together different stone combos into my 'rangs and annihilating everything; I wish there were more viable combos (Fire+Earth leading to explosions that scatter fireballs that also explode, as a dumb example of what could have been) and more opportunities to use them. I loved the characters every minute they were on screen; I wish they were on screen for longer -- so on and so forth.

TY 3 isn't a good game. It's a great game, and if fate had been kinder, it would have been a fantastic one. But the amount of love and care put into it still marks it as something special to me. But hey, much like TY 3, I'm a weirdo. I can't deny that there's a lot of its DNA that appeals to me specifically. But beyond that, it's still TY, and TY's always good.

Even if Sly's still cooler.

Being a huge fan of Ty and Ty 2, I really wanted to love this game. But I can't. Everything it does, Ty 2 did better. 

Playing this game, you can actually feel the budget run out halfway through. Throughout, you'll run 4 mission types

- Ty missions
- Bunyip missions
- Gunyip missions
- Racing missions

Compared to previous entries, these are extremely short, super easy, linear, and repetitive - seriously repetitive, as you'll run a good amount of them more than once. Most of the Ty missions have you walk down a single path just throwing your rangs at enemies mindlessly. I'm almost positive you can get to the end of any of these missions with ease without letting go of the W key (or thumbstick) once, as it is that trivial. The bunyip missions have been reduced to just punching whatever is in front of you, again, with ease. In Ty 2, there were a handful of bunyip models that were assigned to you based on the mission type, allowing for unique scenarios and traversal. That level of design is not present in this game. Gunyip missions did not exist in previous entries, and I'm thankful for that. Compared to the helicopter missions in Ty 2, which had you saving animals or putting out wild fires, they are so boring. Gunyip missions have you shoot whatever is in front of you in a jet that has terrible controls, for a third time, with ease. It just doesn't feel good to fly and the missions are just boring. Lastly, racing missions are no longer just side missions. They are baked into the story, cause somehow we have time to race during an alien invasion. What once were side quests to fill the world with content are now just forced story deviations that make for bad writing and less Ty levels.

The missions being boring and linear aren't even my only complaint. The decision to swap the car from Ty 2 with a "crabmersible" was a horrible one. Good luck moving 20 feet in front of you without flipping or bumping into something. The outbacks of this game are seriously unfun to explore because of that thing.

I can appreciate them trying to update the rang system, but overall, I felt the system present in Ty 2 was better. It felt like a chore having to edit my rangs constantly, looking for a certain ability or combo I wanted.

The world is boring and small compared to Ty 2.

The story is bad and short compared to Ty 2.

The bosses are terrible compared to Ty 2. Seriously, you will fight the same boss 5 times, with nothing changing from the previous fight.

I could go on and on about the smaller things and some other bigger things, but I won't. This review is already long and rambly enough.

Just go play Ty 2.

[h1]A disappointing, unfocused 3D platformer[/h1]
I'm a huge fan of 3D Platformers, and even with a lack of nostalgia for them, I really enjoyed the first two TY games. While I did get some enjoyment out of this third game as well, it's not nearly up to the same level of quality as the other 2 were.

Starting off, TY 3 has a much bigger focus on combat compared to the previous games and it's terrible. While frills can be taken out easily like before, the Quinkan require you to get up close and melee them. Throwing boomerangs won't work, which goes against the entire appeal of using boomerangs as weapons. Not only that, but Quinkan also have big health bars and most of the combat just consists of mashing the attack button over and over again. There are no combo moves to pull off so the combat lacks depth and substance, which gets stale really quickly.

The combat is just as tedious and repetitive as it is broken and exploitative. Once you purchase the Ring Chassis and equip it with 3 Warp stones and 2 Earth stones, you've completely snapped the combat system in half. All enemies, including Quinkan, will go down instantly, and with the warp stones you even get invincibility. You literally don't have to try anymore, meaning there's no reason to engage with the game's combat mechanics or experiment with different Bunyip Stones, which replace the elemental boomerangs from the previous games.

This game also has combat arenas which require you to fight enemies to progress, but unlike the ones from TY 2, these are all mandatory to progress through the story. There's almost nothing to say about these; all you do is fight multiple waves of enemies which already got stale during regular gameplay. Most levels even force combat on you and don't let you progress until all enemies are defeated anyway, so these add nothing to the game at all. I wouldn't even mind forced combat if the combat itself was fun, but sadly it isn't.

Returning from TY 2 are the Shadow and Thermal Bunyips, only these are nowhere near as good as they were in that game. Entire levels are built exclusively for them instead of being built to accommodate for both on foot and Bunyip gameplay, with even worse combat than the regular game. Entire waves of enemies can be defeated instantly as the Thermal Bunyip with the Satellite Strike, but as the Shadow Bunyip, all you can do is mash the attack button until all enemies are defeated, and much like the on foot sections, these levels often lock you into rooms to deal with waves of enemies so there's no avoiding the tedious combat.

I've played other 3D platformers from the PS2 era with really good combat. The Ratchet & Clank games have a wide variety of weapons with each one being useful for different situations, requiring you to think about what weapon works best. Sonic Heroes has a fun combat system with different team formations being more effective against certain enemies. Rayman 2 and 3's combat was also enjoyable as it ties directly into the core platforming. TY 3 lacks a lot of what makes combat in other platformers good even at the time of its release and suffers as a result.

The Crabmersible sounds really cool, but in practice, it's way worse than the Fourbie was. Shooting enemies feels way clunkier than Tails' & Eggman's stages from Sonic Adventure 2 in that you can only target 1 enemy at once so you're spamming the attack button multiple times to defeat entire groups of enemies, and the platforming is atrocious. Multiple times, I have overshot and undershot jumps that would be incredibly simple in any other platformer as the forward momentum is entirely unpredictable. The Crabmersible's platforming and combat felt like an attempt to address the issues with the Fourbie from the previous game, but its execution only made me miss the Fourbie that much more.

Hope you enjoyed the racing mini-games from TY 2, because in this game, they're mandatory to progress. As someone that loved them in the previous game, they're not nearly as good here. Some events require you to defeat all the other racers on the track, but the AI behaves no differently from a regular race so they don't feel right to compete in. The track design is a huge downgrade and weapons are nowhere near as balanced.

New to this game, all of the Gunyip levels are also mandatory. These are plane combat missions where you're mostly just shooting enemy targets to win and are about as fun as they sound. There are powerups, but that doesn't make up for how tedious these missions can get. The final Gunyip mission simply requires reaching the end and can be beaten without firing a single bullet. Variety is nice and all, but am I playing a platformer or an aerial combat game? Because I was actually expecting more 3D platforming from a 3D platformer.

I thought the on foot level design was a huge let down. Previous games had some linear levels mixed in with their more open ended levels, but in TY 3, almost every level is completely linear with barely any exploration involved. There are secrets to find, but it doesn't feel like you're actually exploring levels to find them. The on foot sections control and play similarly to TY 2, but are far worse because of the linearity. Even the 2 HUB areas pale in comparison to Burramudgee Town.

The only good boss fights in this game were the first two. The underwater boss can be defeated just by staying in one spot right in front of it and spamming the attack button; it doesn't even try to attack you directly. The Dragonquin uses the Gunyip and was just as tedious as the other Gunyip missions. The final boss is really frustrating if you don't know how to beat it especially on Hardcore mode, whereas it's super easy yet very long once you know what to do.

Even the PC port of this game is not nearly as good as the ports of the previous games. I experienced several issues that did not exist in the other ports. Frame rate drops were more abundant, at one point a cutscene refused to play when it should displaying an error message, the Crabmersible is very jittery and erratic which can be seizure inducing for some players (which wasn't an issue on PS2) and there were times where the game refused to load an area of the map when using the Crabmersible, requiring me to reset the game to continue.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3318443398

For those planning to play this game on the Steam Deck, this is also a big NO from me as unlike TY 1 and 2, this game does not work on the Steam Deck as the game will crash at a certain point early on in the game, preventing progression. It's obvious to me that there was a lot less love and care put into this PC port compared to TY 1 and 2, making it feel like it was done out of obligation so the entire trilogy could be ported over to PC and not so much because they [i]wanted[/i] to.

This game lacks a clear focus and direction, and from watching the "What Could've Been" video showing a possible TY 4 that was just Gunyip gameplay, it really showed that these developers at the time wanted to chase trends instead of sticking to its platforming roots. A TY 4 that's almost entirely aerial combat doesn't sound like the TY 4 I would want to buy, and it's easy to see why it was cancelled. This studio also worked on The Legend of Spyro A New Beginning and The Eternal Night shortly after this, which only doubled down on this game's tedious combat and linear level design.

I find it really hard to recommend this game, especially when the previous 2 games were really good. It's just okay, which does not fare well when there's other great 3D platformers on Steam like A Hat in Time, Demon Turf, Blue Fire and Psychonauts. The issues with this port also make it difficult for me to recommend if you already own a copy on PS2, GameCube or XBOX. I can only recommend this to fans of the series that want to experience the entire trilogy, and even then, you're better off getting it on sale.

The rangs system got changed, and now they have slots you can equip stones with effects on them. Equipping more stones of a same type, makes the effects stronger. The problem, is that not only sometimes the effects can clash, causing some of them from being lost when equipping another stone, but also isn't very much handy when doing melee combat.
Also, the only way you can check the description of the stone is on the shop screen. There's no way you can check information about the stones outside of it.

This game also features melee combat, which you'll primarily be doing when facing the Quinkans, since they're mostly resistant to simple rang toss. The problem is that melee combat makes your character very vulnerable, and the enemies can parry your attacks (beside you can't parry their attacks). Melee not only makes you more vulnerable, but also hinders your mobility, and there's even a trap room near the end of the game where the developers abuse of that, to make your character be mobbed and killed with ease by the spawning frogs.

I really hated driving around on the outback on the second game, and maybe other people hated it too, but the developers seems to have taken the liberty of adding a worser travelling method for the outback: A mechanical crab vehicle that can end up tumbling with ease whenever you jump.
Not only the tumbling leaves you vulnerable to shots from hostiles whenever it's happening, but also there's jump puzzles that require it! Yes, can you imagine jumping platforms with a vehicle that can begin spinning around after it lands?
Who had the idea?

Beside, the melee doesn't really matter that much in the game, or the rangs, since a good chunk of the stages you do involve you using some vehicle. There's 3 types of vehicle stages:
One where you control a mecha, which you will have to redo with a different type of mecha so you can access some extra places.
One where you do cart races.
One where you fly in a plane.
The worst of the three is the one where you fly in a plane, because it's extremely easy to be shot and colide on anything whenever you're moving. Without counting that the plane is also rather paper.
There's even a boss fight that involves using the plane, which further increased my hate on that vehicle.
Meanwhile, the stages where you control the mecha are generally fun, because beating the quinkans with it is fun.
Doing the boss fight with them isn't though.

Some attacks, mostly involving vehicles, actually either fires faster and gets stronger as you keep pressing the button to use it. It would be nice to know of that, even more on stages where you have to activate generators with the Bunyip.

Speaking of boss fights, they feel really cheap designed to cause you to receive free hits from the boss. There's one where in the first stage, you have to run towards the camera from the boss, but until you process what you have to do, you'll probably get a easy hit, or be so close to the boss that you wont be able to do the mechanic without being hurt.

Also, this game really wants you dead. There's scarcity of health pickups in this game, and the most viable method of recovering Ty's health, is literally by jumping into a lake or something, and make the air counter fill your health bar too.
Seriously, even the vehicle you use on the outback you can restore health by landing on some mission area, while Ty is a lot harder to restore health.
The health pickups actually do drop if you kill a monster, but only if you are on the last health value, and there's still a chance it will not drop. And there's no health bar extension upgrade in this game, so it's literally 4 hits and you're dead.
The penalty for dying in this game... Well... Doesn't really exist, unless on hardcore mode. If you're in a boss fight, the boss will recover part of its health upon respawning.

The cutscenes of the game... Are bad, really bad. After some point on the game story, I begun skipping them due to how cringe they are. Either the dialogue is stupid, or what is happening on the scene is stupid. And the music that plays on them just makes things worser. [spoiler]At least Ty gets a hug from Fluffly... Before bad plot kills her...[/spoiler]
And the ending... Ugh... The ending... No! Don't use the excuse "it's a game for kids". There's a limit on how stupid things can be.

As for the soundtrack? Well... It's actually good. Beside the main menu music has a horrible "ghostly" intro, the follow up is actually good. Actually, I think that in terms of soundtrack, this game excels compared to the prequels.

The most sad thing, is playing the game and noticing the wasted potentials. It's possible to notice on stages where you play as Ty without vehicles, that there are some interesting mechanics that are only used once or twice in the entire game, like throwing a water rang on the water to create a frozen platform. If the game wasn't so brutal regarding how easy it is for your character to lose health compared to gaining, I'd wish some of the minigame stages were instead stages where you play as Ty, and do the classic rang combat, and make use of such mechanics.

The game also has very few secrets in it too. It even feels quite unrewarding to explore. And at some points, the game blocks your way to avoid you from exploring the stage on your story gameplay of it, so not very recommended to try looking for pickups on the first run.

In total, the game has like 2 outback areas, the second one being Cassopolis region, which is a second town you can visit.
I kinda wish there was a third area with a new town, but... This game feels kinda short anyways.
The towns are quite populated with npcs, both new Burramedge and Cassopolis, but I think Cassopolis is more lively due to having npcs actually walking around it. But that's also the lair of the most annoying speedrun puzzle in the game.

I don't recommend playing this game if you want a fun and relaxing gameplay, because this game is really frustrating.
But, if you're like me and wanted to beat the quadrilogy, go ahead. I wish you patience.

Of the entire trilogy, this is the weakest game of them all. And that comes from the simple fact that the devs of old made these titular Quinkan enemies tedious to fight.

The game introduces a melee combat system where if you're close enough to an enemy or a breakable box, you melee them instead of throwing your boomerangs as you had in the previous games. The Quinkan are immune to your regular boomerang attacks, so you must instead melee them.

However, this system feels like such a clunky afterthought of a gameplay mechanic that it makes the Quinkan alot more tedious to fight against. When you're in the thick of things, it's easy for you to run up on a Quinkan to melee it, only to discover you were JUST not close enough to melee, so you end up chucking your boomerang at it (or another enemy instead) and you try to melee it, only for you to bounce back like it blocked you.

And to make matters worse, these suckers are never alone. In the starting areas (atleast as far as I've played), they are always in groups of three or more, and they take 3-7 hits of melee to kill. You yourself could only take 4. That gives these enemies plenty of time to gang up and wipe the floor with you. But it feels as if the game designers wanted you to just focus on one enemy at a time.

And let's not even mention that the Quinkan are atleast HALF of the enemies you're gonna fight in the game. I don't understand - Did the original devs feel like this franchise was too easy or too short? Because this feels like their attempt to pad out the time to beat it or introduce some artificial difficulty. Except that it just ends up being tediously frustrating.

Get the other two games while they're on sale, and avoid this one. Those two are actually fun.

-Best collection screen setup

The game that introduced me to the series as a kid, and thus gets free rose-tinted glasses for life, but has objectively bad changes from the previous games. Chief among them being that this game practically followed a "how to make your combat worse" guide and strongly incentivizes you to simply make a room-clearing-explosion custom 'rang as soon as possible using earth stones because your alternative is most enemies simply blocking your attacks until you melee them or taking much longer to kill otherwise. This leads to there only being two boomerangs in the game that matter for you: the one with the rope and the one that has the most customization slots (though you don't need all of them). At least in 2 they made this way of fighting less universally practical because of how the different 'rangs would fly until the late-game, though of course these aren't very deep games.

I personally like the greater variety in mission types and gameplay, but it is unfortunate that the bunyip missions simply reuse the same map with different starting locations. The bosses in this game aren't bad per se, but get reused a bunch, which is boring and a pain. 

I do really like the atmosphere and detail of the levels this time around though, and the music remains great. The crabmersible which replaces the truck as the method of transport between areas is also way more fun and versatile. The collectibles in this game tend to be more visible than in previous entries, with the challenge being more getting to them, which I don't mind at all. Overall this game feels a bit shorter and less polished than the second game, but is still a fun game.
